title: Pac-Man
description: Pac-Man arrived in 1980 and changed what an arcade game could be about. Instead of shooting, the player steered a round hero through a maze, eating dots while four ghosts with distinct personalities patrolled the corridors. Large power pellets briefly let the hero turn the tables and hunt the ghosts, and the game's cheerful look drew in players who had never touched a shooter.
body:
Pac-Man arrived in 1980 and changed what an arcade game could be about. Instead of shooting, the player steered a round hero through a maze, eating dots while four ghosts with distinct personalities patrolled the corridors. Large power pellets briefly let the hero turn the tables and hunt the ghosts, and the game's cheerful look drew in players who had never touched a shooter.

This tribute recreates the maze chase with a winding corridor map, a full field of dots, and a single pursuing ghost. The demo changes the original by shrinking the ghost cast to one pursuer and scripting a clean route through the maze, so the dot-eating rhythm is easy to follow. It is an original tribute inspired by the mechanics, not the game itself.

Maze runners learn the map before they chase the score. Clear the edges early, memorize the escape routes from every corner, and never enter a corridor you cannot leave. The players who lasted longest treated the maze as a place they lived in, not a puzzle they solved once.

title: Ms. Pac-Man
description: Ms. Pac-Man arrived in 1982 as a sequel that improved nearly everything about the maze chase: faster movement, new maze layouts, moving bonus fruit that traveled through the maze, and ghosts that behaved less predictably. It became one of the best-selling arcade games of all time, and many players remember it more fondly than the original.
body:
Ms. Pac-Man arrived in 1982 as a sequel that improved nearly everything about the maze chase: faster movement, new maze layouts, moving bonus fruit that traveled through the maze, and ghosts that behaved less predictably. It became one of the best-selling arcade games of all time, and many players remember it more fondly than the original.

This tribute recreates the maze chase with a fresh corridor map, its own dot pattern, and a single pursuing ghost starting in a different corner. The demo changes the original by scripting one route through the new maze, so the differences in layout and dot placement can be compared directly with the first game. It is an original tribute inspired by the mechanics.

The sequel rewards bolder routing. Because the hero moves faster, a runner can cut across the maze's middle lanes where the original game punished such risks. Learn the new map's shortcuts, take the middle lanes when the ghost is far, and the maze opens up in ways the first game never allowed.

title: Pac-Mania
description: Pac-Mania arrived in 1987 as a three-dimensional take on the maze chase, showing the maze at a slant so the hero could jump over ghosts. The jump button changed everything: a well-timed hop cleared a pursuer entirely, and the mazes grew taller and more layered. It was the series' boldest visual reinvention, and it kept the chase fresh for a new generation.
body:
Pac-Mania arrived in 1987 as a three-dimensional take on the maze chase, showing the maze at a slant so the hero could jump over ghosts. The jump button changed everything: a well-timed hop cleared a pursuer entirely, and the mazes grew taller and more layered. It was the series' boldest visual reinvention, and it kept the chase fresh for a new generation.

This tribute recreates the maze chase on a tall, roomy map with its own dot pattern and ghost start, played from the classic top-down view. The demo changes the original by scripting a route without jumping, since the tribute engine moves in four directions only, so the chase is shown in its pure form: dots, lanes, and one relentless pursuer. It is an original tribute inspired by the mechanics.

Even without jumping, the lesson of the later maze games holds: keep moving, keep an escape lane open, and never let the ghost dictate your route. The jump was a new tool, but the old skills, map memory and calm routing, still decided who cleared the maze.

title: Dig Dug
description: Dig Dug arrived in 1982 as a digging game: the player tunneled through underground soil, inflating enemies until they popped and dropping rocks on those that chased too closely. The maze was not fixed but carved by the player, and the game rewarded clever digging, trapping enemies in dead ends and planning an escape before the pump ran out.
body:
Dig Dug arrived in 1982 as a digging game: the player tunneled through underground soil, inflating enemies until they popped and dropping rocks on those that chased too closely. The maze was not fixed but carved by the player, and the game rewarded clever digging, trapping enemies in dead ends and planning an escape before the pump ran out.

This tribute adapts the digging maze to a dot-eating maze map, and the adaptation is stated honestly: the tunnels here are fixed in advance rather than carved by the player, and the dots stand in for the soil and rewards of the original dig. A single pursuer stands in for the underground chase. It is an original tribute inspired by the mechanics, not the game itself.

Digging wisdom applies even in a fixed maze: never dig yourself into a corner, always leave a second tunnel out, and let the pursuer come to you rather than chasing it. The players who lasted longest underground were the ones who planned their tunnels before they needed them.

This tribute recreates the maze chase on its own frozen-field map with a distinct dot pattern and ghost start, using the dots to mark the field's open ice. Ice mazes reward thinking in lines. A push that lines up two blocks is worth more than two pushes that scatter them, and a runner who plans the field before moving clears it faster than one who pushes at random. Plan the line, then make the move.

title: Wizard of Wor
description: Wizard of Wor arrived in 1980 as a maze shooter: two players explored dungeon mazes, shooting monsters that appeared in the corridors, while the wizard himself eventually appeared to hunt them. The dungeons changed layout, the monsters grew faster, and the game mixed maze exploration with arcade shooting in a way no earlier maze game had attempted.
body:
Wizard of Wor arrived in 1980 as a maze shooter: two players explored dungeon mazes, shooting monsters that appeared in the corridors, while the wizard himself eventually appeared to hunt them. The dungeons changed layout, the monsters grew faster, and the game mixed maze exploration with arcade shooting in a way no earlier maze game had attempted.

This tribute is a maze game with a shooter element, and the blend is stated honestly: the maze engine moves in four directions and eats dots, so the dots stand in for cleared dungeon corridors, and the single pursuer stands in for the dungeon's monsters. The shooting itself is described here rather than simulated, because the tribute engine does not fire. It is an original tribute inspired by the mechanics.

Dungeon mazes reward clearing as you go. A corridor you have already walked is a safe retreat, while an unexplored corridor may hold anything, so the wise adventurer advances one corridor at a time and never lets the retreat close behind them.
controls: Type up/down/left/right to move, quit to stop.

title: Bomberman
description: Bomberman arrived in 1987 as a maze game with bombs: the player walked a grid maze, laid bombs to blast blocks and enemies, and collected power-ups that lengthened the blasts and quickened the pace. The single-player maze was only the beginning; the game's multiplayer battles, with four players trapping each other in bomb blasts, became legendary.
body:
Bomberman arrived in 1987 as a maze game with bombs: the player walked a grid maze, laid bombs to blast blocks and enemies, and collected power-ups that lengthened the blasts and quickened the pace. The single-player maze was only the beginning; the game's multiplayer battles, with four players trapping each other in bomb blasts, became legendary.

This tribute is a maze game with a bomb element, and the blend is stated honestly: the maze engine moves in four directions and eats dots, so the dots stand in for blasted blocks and cleared ground, and the single pursuer stands in for the maze's enemies. The bomb-laying itself is described here rather than simulated, because the tribute engine does not place bombs. It is an original tribute inspired by the mechanics.

Bomb mazes reward blast awareness: never stand where your own blast will reach, always leave an escape corridor before you strike, and use the maze's walls as shields. The players who mastered the grid were the ones who thought one blast ahead, and the runner here should think one corridor ahead.
controls: Type up/down/left/right to move, quit to stop.
